title: Complete, Bipartite and Cycle Graphs
short: Kₙ has n(n − 1)/2 edges, K(m, n) has mn, and the cycle Cₙ has n.
trouble: Students count the edges of Kₙ as n(n − 1), counting each edge once from each end.

blocks.html: A few graphs come up so often that they have names. Knowing their edge counts and degrees saves time, and each count is a small exercise in the handshake lemma or in combinations.

The complete graph $K_{n}$ joins every pair of its $n$ vertices: $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ edges, every degree $n - 1$. The complete bipartite graph $K_{m,n}$ has two sides of $m$ and $n$ vertices, with every vertex joined to every vertex on the other side and none on its own: $mn$ edges. The cycle $C_{n}$ ($n \ge 3$) is a ring of $n$ vertices with $n$ edges; the path $P_{n}$ is $n$ vertices in a row with $n - 1$ edges.

An edge of $K_{n}$ is a choice of two endpoints, so there are $\binom{n}{2} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ of them. The handshake lemma agrees: $n$ vertices of degree $n - 1$ give a degree sum of $n(n - 1)$, which is twice the number of edges. In $K_{m,n}$ an edge is one choice from each side, so the product rule gives $mn$.

blocks.html: Each row passes the handshake test. For $K_{m,n}$: $m$ vertices of degree $n$ and $n$ vertices of degree $m$ give a degree sum of $2mn$, twice the edge count. For $P_{n}$: $1 + 1 + 2(n - 2) = 2(n - 1)$.

blocks.title: Working backward
blocks.q: A complete graph has $66$ edges. How many vertices does it have?
steps: Two consecutive integers with product $132$: $12 \cdot 11$. So $n = 12$.

blocks.title: Which are bipartite?
blocks.q: A graph is bipartite when its vertices split into two sides with every edge going between the sides. Are $C_{6}$, $C_{5}$ and $K_{2,4}$ bipartite?
steps: $C_{6}$: color the vertices alternately around the ring; six is even, so the last vertex differs from the first. Bipartite.
$C_{5}$: alternating around a ring of five ends with two neighbors on the same side. Not bipartite.
$K_{2,4}$: bipartite by definition, with its two sides.

blocks.cap: $K_{3,3}$: two sides of three, $3 \cdot 3 = 9$ edges, and no edges inside a side.

blocks.html: Counting the edges of $K_{n}$ as $n(n - 1)$. Adding up "each vertex is joined to $n - 1$ others" counts every edge twice, once from each end. Check: for $K_{3}$, a triangle, the formula must give $3$, not $6$.
